episodes.192584: Scattered to numerous evening thunderstorms tracking mainly eastward across central Indiana, included 5 severe cells that altogether produced widely scattered wind damage.  More pronounced rotation was exhibited by a few storms crossing northeastern central Indiana, with a funnel cloud near the ground in Henry County, before a tornado that started as an EF0 in Hamilton County, which tracked for 3 miles into Madison County, peaking at EF2 intensity just before dissipating.
episodes.192585: A small line of severe storms crossing east-central Illinois bowed out while crossing far southwestern central Indiana.  Steep 0-1 km lapse rates and high amounts of low-level moisture promoted severe winds reaching the surface within the core of the cells.  Widespread 50-55 mph winds included embedded, isolated damaging winds from the strongest gusts in Knox and Daviess Counties.
episodes.192666: A large storm trekking across western into southern portions of the state crossed through Jones county with up to tennis-ball sized hail and damaging winds. The Jones county sheriff reported several hail damaged vehicles on Interstate 90, and that strong winds had flipped over some campers and knocked over motorcyclists. A CoCoRaHS observer 12 miles west of Murdo measured the hail at 2.5 inches. While other storms were in the area, few other reports of severe weather occurred with these storms, with the most notable being the weather station 2 miles north of Harreid (Campbell county) recording a wind gust of 70 mph. USDA crop indemnities for Jones county topped 188 thousand dollars.
episodes.192698: An approaching cold front combined with a hot and humid air mass sparked a severe thunderstorm across Amherst County and the independent city of Lynchburg.  Winds from this storm blew down two trees.
episodes.192758: Two lines of thunderstorms moved through Middle Tennessee on July 30, 2024. One of these lines moved through the area during the afternoon while the second arrived late in the evening. Damaging winds were the primary threat with these thunderstorms with numerous reports of downed trees and power lines received. Heavy rain was also reported across the Cumberland Plateau with flooding occurring in portions of Putnam and White counties. In Williamson County, a lightning strike caused a house fire which caused smoke inhalation for four firefighters.
episodes.192788: An upper level shortwave coupled with strong wind fields brought multiple rounds of severe weather to East Tennessee, including two mesoscale convective systems. Flash flooding occurred in Knox county.
episodes.192789: An upper level shortwave brings an evening mesoscale convective system to southwest North Carolina.
episodes.192795: A cluster of strong to severe thunderstorms developed along the nose of the nocturnal low-level jet in eastern Nebraska during the late evening of July 29th...then tracked southeastward across south-central Illinois during the morning of July 30th.  The storms produced sporadic wind damage along and south of a Macomb...to Lincoln...to Lawrenceville line.
episodes.192804: A Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) that formed over eastern Nebraska and western Iowa during the pre-dawn hours of July 30th decayed as it tracked southeastward toward the Mississippi River.  As it moved further southeastward, it re-intensified across south-central Illinois during peak heating.  The newly formed cluster of storms produced scattered wind damage and a few hailstones as large as quarters along and south of a Lincoln...to Mattoon...to Lawrenceville line during the afternoon of July 30th.
episodes.192818: Scattered thunderstorms moved across parts of east central Illinois during the evening of July 29th producing two funnel clouds.
episodes.192927: An area of thunderstorms resulted in strong winds and areas of flash flooding in southern Cochise County.
episodes.193019: An upper level disturbance moving southeast across the region produced showers and thunderstorms during the evening hours.
episodes.193020: An upper level disturbance moving southeast across the region produced showers and thunderstorms during the early morning hours.
episodes.193021: An upper level disturbance moving southeast across the region produced showers and thunderstorms during the overnight hours.
episodes.193049: Scattered slow moving thunderstorms produced isolated instances of trees down and flash flooding.
episodes.193104: An area of low pressure supported widespread showers and thunderstorms on July 30th and 31st. Slow storm motions allowed heavy rain to fall over the same area, with high rainfall rates over 2 inches per hour.  The most significant flooding occurred over Grafton County where saturated ground conditions and steep terrain supported flash flooding in Piermont.
episodes.193322: Diurnal instability with sea breeze and upper-level short wave trough forcing triggered strong to severe storms with locally heavy across SE GA in the afternoon and evening.
episodes.193476: Northwesterly flow set up across the Carolinas in late July, with several shortwaves pushing over the Appalachians and forcing widespread convection. With significant instability in place on the afternoon of July 30, several strong to severe thunderstorms developed across central SC and east central GA. These resulted in hail and wind damage reports, as well as some isolated flash flooding.
episodes.193778: Thunderstorms developed over northern Cherry County and south central South Dakota during the early evening hours of July 29th. This activity became severe just north of Valentine around 7 PM CDT. As this activity tracked to the east-southeast, it remained severe through around 10 PM CDT exiting Boyd county to the east. Overnight, strong winds in association with a convective induced heat burst, impacted the Keystone and Lemoyne  areas with winds of 65 to 75 MPH.
episodes.193804: Convergent and moist south-southeast flow in the low-levels over South Florida supported the development of scattered showers across the local Gulf waters on the morning of July 30th.
episodes.193831: Thunderstorms developed along an outflow boundary during the late afternoon and early evening hours on Tuesday (7/30).  The strongest storms produced large hail up to 1 inch across central and north-central Wisconsin.
episodes.193847: Moderate instability under an upper level area of low pressure across northern VT during the afternoon of July 30th led to scattered thunderstorms with isolated tree damage.
episodes.193850: Moderate instability under an upper level area of low pressure across northern VT during the afternoon of July 30th led to isolated thunderstorms with one damage report in Moriah.
episodes.193952: Thunderstorms ahead of a cold front produced locally heavy rainfall that led to an isolated instance of flash flooding in Warren County.
episodes.194009: Early morning thunderstorms produced a waterspout off the west end of Panama City Beach on July 30th. Later in the day, strong thunderstorm wind gusts impacted the St George Island Bridge.
episodes.194149: A complex of thunderstorms moved across the Northland during the morning of the 30th. While primarily bringing heavy rainfall as it moved through, some gusty winds with the storms did bring down a tree near Hayward to partially blocked a roadway. Otherwise, the storms were non-severe across the region.
episodes.194157: A large supercell thunderstorm developed over southern Haakon County and tracked east-southeast across south central South Dakota. The storm produced large hail and damaging wind gusts across the area, including significant damage in the Winner area.
episodes.194160: A supercell thunderstorm tracked across southern Todd County before weakening as it moved into Tripp County. The storm produced large hail to golf ball size east of St. Francis.
episodes.194161: A supercell thunderstorm over northern Meade County produced large hail and strong winds southeast of Faith.
episodes.194162: A supercell thunderstorm developed over eastern Pennington County and tracked east-southeast into Haakon County, producing large hail and wind gusts to over 60 mph. A brief funnel cloud was reported northwest of Philip as well.
episodes.194187: Multiple rounds of severe storms impacted Iowa on July 30th. This first round occurred through the early morning as a bowing line of storms moved into the area from Nebraska around 1 am CDT. This passed across the area through the early morning hours, exiting into southeastern Iowa by 5 am. Several sites reported wind gusts of 60-65 mph as this line of storms swept across the area. A second bowing segment passed across the are in the mid to late morning, this time bringing hail along with the winds. In its wake, thunderstorms developed on the outflow boundary across central to southeast Iowa. These storms were slow moving and produced heavy rain along with a number of quarter sized and larger hail reports.
episodes.194239: Storms developed during the early morning hours across northeast Missouri and produced damaging wind gusts in Clark and Scotland Counties.
episodes.194243: Thunderstorms developed in northeast Missouri and west central Illinois and produced damaging wind gusts as they moved into McDonough County.
episodes.194396: Thunderstorms dove southeastward through Southern Illinois during the late evening hours on the 29th. A few of these storms produced damaging wind gusts, downing trees and powerlines. MLCAPE fell from 3000 to 1500 J/kg over the course of the evening, while DCAPE remained around 1200 J/kg. Effective bulk shear was approximately 35 kts.
episodes.194397: A particularly explosive storm environment developed on the afternoon of the 30th. MLCAPE values rose to 3500-4000 J/kg, 0-3 km CAPE of 100-150 J/kg, effective bulk shear of 30-40 kts, and 0-3 km shear of 20-30 kts. Temperatures rose to the low 90s with dew points in the upper 70s to near 80, yielding heat index values near 110. For Southern Illinois, an MCS dove southeastward during the afternoon, producing sporadic thunderstorm wind damage.
episodes.194398: A particularly explosive storm environment developed on the afternoon of the 30th. MLCAPE values rose to 3500 J/kg, 0-3 km CAPE of 100-150 J/kg, effective bulk shear of 40 kts, and 0-3 km shear of 20-30 kts. Temperatures rose to the low 90s with dew points in the upper 70s to near 80, yielding heat index values near 110. For Southwest Indiana, the storms moved through late afternoon towards sunset. A more complex setup occurred relative to Illinois and Kentucky. A robust cluster of storms moved southeastward through Gibson County towards Evansville, bringing down trees and powerlines in Patoka and Princeton while damaging corn. A semi truck was overturned at the Toyota plant south of Princeton. Meanwhile, a north-south line of storms moving into Posey County accelerated eastward into Evansville with widespread reports of wind damage in Vanderburgh County. Near Melody Hill, just east of the airport, the intersecting boundary with these two clusters spun up an EF-1 tornado that tracked southeastward into Warrick County lifting northeast of Newburgh. Straight-line wind damage occurred in Warrick County north and south of the tornado track. The following day, one person (65m) passed away due to a heart attack sustained while cleaning up tree debris in Newburgh.
episodes.194399: A particularly explosive storm environment developed on the afternoon of the 30th. MLCAPE values rose to 3500-4000 J/kg, 0-3 km CAPE of 100-150 J/kg, effective bulk shear of 30-40 kts, and 0-3 km shear of 20-30 kts. Temperatures rose to the low 90s with dew points in the upper 70s to near 80, yielding heat index values near 110. For Western Kentucky, an MCS dove southeastward during the evening, producing sporadic thunderstorm wind damage, mainly tree damage with a couple instances of structure damage.
episodes.194543: A cluster of nearly stationary thunderstorms affected portions of Caledonia, Essex and Orleans Counties in northeastern Vermont during the early to mid morning hours of July 30, 2024. This produced rainfall amounts from 4 to as much as 8 inches in these areas which led to severe, and in some cases catastrophic flash flooding. The department of highways, state/local emergency management, and NWS Storm Surveys confirmed the hardest hit areas were in the towns of Morgan, Lyndon and St. Johnsbury, VT. Preliminary assessments show five bridges destroyed, five homes destroyed, damage to 20 to 30 additional homes, and numerous roads washed out. Total damage costs will likely near or exceed $10 million dollars.
episodes.194554: Slow moving thunderstorms produced localized rainfall amounts of two to three inches in the Rutland/Clarendon, VT area during late afternoon/early evening of July 29, 2024. A few reports of high water and flash flooding were received.
episodes.194563: A mid-level trough tracking across the area, along with plenty of instability of 2,000 J/kg or more of CAPE resulted in the formation of thunderstorms across the region. As storms tracked northeast across the Finger Lakes area during the afternoon, a storm produced damage in Geneva. Shear with this setup was limited, resulting in less severe thunderstorms than would have otherwise been possible. Even though there were a few rounds of convection, nearly all of the thunderstorms remained below severe limits.
episodes.194656: Broken remnants of an MCS moved out of the Midwest towards the Southeast. A few storms within the system were able to produce damaging wind gusts along an extended length. A few thunderstorms ahead of the line also developed which were also capable of strong to damaging winds.
episodes.194657: An MCS out of the north produced widespread thunderstorms winds damage from North GA down between Columbus and Macon. One of the downed trees fell on a car, sadly resulting in 1 fatality.
episodes.194693: Thunderstorms initially formed in the late afternoon in the vicinity of a surface boundary over southwest North Dakota, with additional storms then forming through the late afternoon into the evening in an environment of elevated instability and deep layer shear. Many storms became supercells, producing very large hail. Over the Bismarck-Mandan area, three separate storms produced large hail. The first storm passed through the Harmon Lake area before crossing the Missouri River and passing through the north side of Bismarck, causing extensive damage with hail up to 3 inches in diameter. As that storm moved along, a second storm formed to the south of Mandan and quickly intensified as it crossed the Missouri River and passed over developments to the south of Bismarck and over the Lincoln area. Many locations experienced two inch diameter hail with this storm, which increased to baseball size over Lincoln. One mile south of Lincoln, a hailstone was measured at 4.5 inches. These two storms caused extensive damage to structures and vehicles, resulting in millions of dollars in damage. A third severe storm then formed over Bismarck, but this storm was weaker, producing one-inch diameter hail. Additional thunderstorms then continued over central North Dakota with the main threat shifting towards strong winds late in the event. The strongest wind gust was estimated at 75 mph at McKenna Lake, near Napoleon, Logan County, where four campers were blown over.
episodes.194695: Thunderstorms formed near and ahead of a weak surface low over western North Dakota along a weak warm front, with some storms becoming severe. The strongest wind gust estimated at 75 mph occurred at Hazen in Mercer County where tree damage was reported. The largest reported hail was one-inch in diameter, occurring around Minot and to the north of Rice Lake in Ward County.
episodes.194768: Afternoon thunderstorms associated with the sea breeze produce wind damage near Bradenton in Manatee County.
episodes.194769: Thunderstorms associated with the sea breeze produce a late morning water spout offshore Sanibel in Lee County and an evening water spout offshore Port Richey in Pasco County.
episodes.194829: Thunderstorms moved into southeast Iowa during the morning hours of July 30th and produced damaging winds as they moved across the area.
episodes.194833: Supercell thunderstorms developed along a boundary, situated along the South Dakota and Nebraska border during the late afternoon of July 30th. As this initial activity tracked to the southeast, it quickly became severe as it traversed northeastern Cherry and Keya Paha counties into Brown and Rock counties. Hail up to 2 inches in diameter and a tornado was reported near Ainsworth.
episodes.194836: A mesoscale convective vorticity maximum tracked across central MN and produced an outflow boundary that converged with a nose of instability. This caused an isolated cell to briefly produce hen egg sized hail over southeastern Polk County before it quickly weakened.
episodes.194853: Thunderstorms developed during the mid afternoon and produced damaging winds in Keokuk and Jefferson Counties.
episodes.194854: On July 30th, a cold front was positioned just north of the state, with a weak secondary boundary noted across the east-central portion of the state. In addition, a shortwave was also passing through the Ohio Valley, increasing the lift and mixing. The Storm Prediction Center placed a Slight Risk for severe weather across the western half of the state and locations to the NW. At the surface, a line of storms (MCS) moved through eastern Kentucky during the early morning hours, with more individual cells developing behind the line during the mid morning hours. Closer to the frontal boundary to our NW in Illinois, another area of storms developed during the morning hours and started shifting southeast, creating a second MCS. The Storm Prediction Center went ahead and included south-central KY in a Severe Thunderstorm Watch just after 2pm EDT as the MCS moved southeast into Kentucky, including the SW portions of the Jackson CWA. The MCS rolled into south-eastern Kentucky by the mid afternoon, with damaging wind gusts being the primary concern. This stayed true to the watch, as a handful of counties in the SW, including Rockcastle, Pulaski Laurel, Clay and McCreary all received severe thunderstorm winds. Unfortunately this event also resulted in an injury, when a tree fell at a Pulaski County camp ground.
episodes.194868: Strong to severe thunderstorms worked their way east from western North Dakota in the early morning hours of July 30th. Main hazards were large hail and wind damage in lakes country Minnesota.
episodes.194869: Strong to severe thunderstorms worked their way east from western North Dakota in the early morning hours of July 30th. Main hazards were large hail and wind damage in lakes country Minnesota, as well as the southern Red River Valley.
episodes.194912: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed across western North Carolina, mainly during the late afternoon and evening. Several of the storms produced brief swaths of damaging wind gusts. Meanwhile, training thunderstorms resulted in very heavy rainfall and flash flooding in Henderson County.
episodes.194916: Scattered thunderstorms developed over upstate South Carolina throughout the afternoon and evening. A few of the storms produced damaging wind gusts, mainly in the evening.
episodes.195080: A progressive cluster of thunderstorms developed across south central South Dakota in response to a weak mid-level wave drifting out of western South Dakota. A slight increase in the low-level jet brought deep-layer shear to 35-40 knots, and MUCAPE around 2000 J/kg provided fuel for storms to strengthen and congeal into a bowing structure which traversed to the east-southeast. The strongest storms produced damaging winds generally from 60 to 80 mph. In the wake of the evening convection, scattered elevated storms developed, which produced a combination of damaging winds and spotty large hail during the very early morning hours of July 30.
episodes.195083: A progressive cluster of thunderstorms developed across south central South Dakota in response to a weak mid-level wave drifting out of western South Dakota. A slight increase in the low-level jet brought deep-layer shear to 35-40 knots, and MUCAPE around 2000 J/kg provided fuel for storms to strengthen and congeal into a bowing structure which traversed to the east-southeast. The strongest storms produced damaging winds generally from 60 to 80 mph.
episodes.195084: A progressive cluster of thunderstorms developed across south central South Dakota in response to a weak mid-level wave drifting out of western South Dakota. A slight increase in the low-level jet brought deep-layer shear to 35-40 knots, and MUCAPE around 2000 J/kg provided fuel for storms to strengthen and congeal into a bowing structure which traversed to the east-southeast. The strongest storms produced damaging winds generally from 60 to 80 mph.
episodes.195182: The prevailing upper-level pattern for the end of July featured a trough over the Pacific Northwest, favoring southwesterly flow over the central Great Plains. Two troughs ejected out into the north-central CONUS during this episode. The first brought two back to back nights of severe weather across portions of northeast Nebraska the night of the 28th and the 29th. The second trough moved out into the central Plains and brought the synoptic scale forcing for a historic severe wind event that impacted both Lincoln and Omaha metropolitan areas. Wind gusts as high as 100 miles per hour extended from Lancaster County northeast to the Nebraska-Iowa border, leaving behind a large swath of significant tree, powerline and structural damage. Power outages from this storm lasted for up to a week in some locations, particularly in Omaha. ||This episode also featured several afternoons of excessive heat for portions of southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa. A few instances of 110 degree heat indices were observed in a few southwest Iowa counties the afternoon of the 29th, with even more widespread excessive heat the afternoon of the 31st across much of the forecast area south of Interstate 80. Peak heat indices in this region topped out between 110 and 115 degrees before afternoon convection cooled temperatures back down.
episodes.195183: The prevailing upper-level pattern for the end of July featured a trough over the Pacific Northwest, favoring southwesterly flow over the central Great Plains. Two troughs ejected out into the north-central CONUS during this episode. The first brought two back to back nights of severe weather across portions of northeast Nebraska the night of the 28th and the 29th. The second trough moved out into the central Plains and brought the synoptic scale forcing for a historic severe wind event that impacted both Lincoln and Omaha metropolitan areas. Wind gusts as high as 100 miles per hour extended from Lancaster County northeast to the Nebraska-Iowa border, leaving behind a large swath of significant tree, powerline and structural damage. episodes.195226: A stationary front was located over the lower Ohio Valley from July 30th into July 31st, with upper level flow oriented from northwest to southeast across the region. This upper flow pattern brought multiple waves of showers and thunderstorms across southern Indiana and central Kentucky over this two day stretch. Scattered strong to severe storms mainly produced wind damage, with localized flash flooding also being reported where there was training of multiple rounds of showers and storms.

The tornado began as an EF0 with damage to the roof of a metal barn and uprooted trees along Strawtown Road, just west of Indiana State Road 13 in Hamilton County. The tornado skipped over SR 13 into Madison County where it continued for another 2.6 miles while intensifying to an EF2.  The tornado's maximum width of 50 yards occurred in Madison County.

The tornado began in far eastern Hamilton County as an EF0 before skipping across Indiana Route 13 into Madison County and quickly landing in a field at a cemetery south of Perkinsville in Madison county, causing sporadic tree damage. The tornado crossed the White River, snapping and uprooting several trees at a residence south of County Road 300 North where it was rated an EF1. The tornado then moved into a corn field before lifting briefly prior to hitting the Frankton Lapel Administration Building where significant brick wall and roof damage occurred. The roof of a small gymnasium at this building was lifted and thrown approximately 150 yards to the north northeast while the western brick wall collapsed inward. Numerous concrete masonry blocks were thrown from the wall into the top of several school buses that also sustained damage. One bus had a small but long metal support driven through the frame. The tornado was rated EF2 here before it continued into a corn field to the northeast and dissipated.
Large tree down at Rowe Road and Hutchinson Road.

The tornado began along a wooded area west of Holland Road and south of Oxford Pike. Drone footage revealed broken branches and convergent swirls within crops along the wooded area. The tornado continued northeast, remaining west of Holland Road. A property near the intersection of Holland Road and Oxford Pike received minor damage. An outbuilding sustained roof panel loss and the residence had minor roof damage along with blown out windows. Tree damage observed around the property was also convergent. The damage to and around the property suggested estimated peak winds|around 75 mph. The tornado entered an open field north of Oxford Pike, where tornadic swirls were evident within the crops. This was the final evidence of the tornado and it is believed to have quickly dissipated north of Oxford Pike.

An EF-1 tornado began just east of Evansville Regional Airport in the Melody Hill Community as intersecting boundaries met up with a surge in the storm line. After uprooting trees near the Oak Hill School, the tornado moved east-southeastward, damaging light fixtures and destroying a structure at the Goebel Soccer Complex. The tornado crossed I-69, eventually entering into Warrick County. Estimated peak winds for the Vanderburgh County portion of the tornado were 105 mph.

An EF-1 tornado that began just east of the Evansville Regional Airport tracked east-southeastward, crossing from Vanderburgh County to Warrick County. The tornado crossed several fields before reaching more populated neighborhoods from Bell Rd onward. The majority of the damage was caused by downed trees and large tree limbs. Several trees fell into homes causing damage. A few homes also suffered roof and gutter damage. There was very substantial tree damage along Telephone Rd to Fuquay Rd. The tornado eventually lifted between Wethers Rd and IN-61 in the Victoria Hills area. Estimated peak winds for the Warrick County portion, and the tornado as a whole, were 110 mph.
